Spatial prediction from a fitted RiskMap model

Source: R/spatial_prediction.R
predict.RiskMap.Rd

Predicts the latent spatial process, linear predictor and response-scale distribution at observed or new locations. New locations and every variable required by the fitted model are supplied together in one sf object, keeping their rows aligned.

Usage

# S3 method for class 'RiskMap'
predict(
  object,
  newdata = NULL,
  boundaries = NULL,
  aggregate = NULL,
  type = c("auto", "marginal", "joint"),
  include = NULL,
  transform = NULL,
  standardize = NULL,
  summaries = c("mean", "lower", "upper"),
  thresholds = NULL,
  level = 0.95,
  weights = NULL,
  control_mcmc = NULL,
  parameter_uncertainty = FALSE,
  parameter_draws = 50L,
  seed = NULL,
  keep_samples = FALSE,
  messages = getOption("RiskMap.messages", TRUE),
  ...
)

Arguments

object

A fitted RiskMap object returned by glgpm().

newdata

An sf object with point geometries and the variables needed by the fitted model. When NULL, predictions are made at the observed locations.

boundaries

Optional sf polygon object. When supplied, prediction locations are assigned to polygons and their joint samples are aggregated within each polygon. Grids returned by create_grid() use exact fractional cell coverage; other point objects use point-in-polygon assignment.

aggregate

Character vector naming one or more within-polygon operations: "mean", "median", "sum", "min", or "max". It must be supplied when boundaries is used. Several operations reuse the same joint predictive samples. Custom operations can be supplied in a named list, optionally mixed with built-ins, for example list(mean = "mean", q90 = function(values, weights) ...). A custom function receives a location-by-draw matrix and the location weights and must return one numeric value per draw.

type

Character string specifying "auto", "marginal", or "joint" prediction. "auto" uses marginal prediction for locations and joint prediction when boundaries are supplied.

include

NULL, or a character vector specifying optional components to add to the complete linear predictor and response. Supported values are "random_effects", for conditional predictions at known groups, and "nugget", for a new realization of observation-level predictive variation at locations supplied through newdata. Fixed effects, the spatial process and any offset are always returned separately.

transform

Optional named list of functions defining derived predictive targets from the complete linear-predictor draws. Each function receives a location-by-draw matrix and must return a numeric matrix with the same dimensions. The ordinary response-scale prediction is always calculated, so this argument is needed only for additional scientific targets, for example list(stunting = function(link) pnorm((-2 - link) / sd_child)).

standardize

Optional data frame describing a common reference population over which response-scale predictions are averaged. Its columns must be fixed-effect predictors from the fitted model and override the corresponding columns in newdata. Rows receive equal weight unless an optional numeric .weight column is supplied. Predictor values kept together on each row are standardized jointly, preserving their empirical association. This answers what would be predicted if every location had the same reference-population distribution. .weight weights reference people or profiles and is distinct from the polygon weights argument.

summaries

Character vector naming the summaries calculated from each predictive distribution. Supported values are "mean", "median", "sd", "cv", "lower", "upper", "interval_width", and "exceedance". The coefficient of variation is calculated only on the response scale and is returned as NA when the predictive mean is non-positive or numerically too close to zero for a stable ratio. Custom summaries can be supplied in a named list, optionally mixed with built-ins, for example list(mean = "mean", iqr = IQR). Each custom function receives the predictive draws and must return one numeric value.

thresholds

Numeric thresholds used when summaries includes "exceedance". One exceedance probability is returned for each threshold on the response scale and for every target supplied through transform.

level

Number strictly between zero and one giving the probability covered by the "lower" and "upper" interval limits and used to calculate "interval_width".

weights

NULL for equally weighted polygon summaries, or the name of a numeric column in newdata containing non-negative location weights. For aggregate = "mean" or "median", weights are interpreted within each polygon. A weighted median is returned when weights are supplied. For aggregate = "sum", their original scale is retained. Weights do not affect "min" or "max".

control_mcmc

Optional output from set_control_mcmc(). When omitted, conditional samples stored in a non-Gaussian fit are reused. Supplying a control object requests a fresh conditional run.

parameter_uncertainty

Logical. If FALSE (the default), predictions are made at the estimated parameters (plug-in prediction). If TRUE, they also reflect the uncertainty in the estimated parameters; see Details.

parameter_draws

Positive integer giving the number of parameter values drawn when parameter_uncertainty = TRUE. Default 50. Conditional samples stored in the fit are not used in that case, because they condition on the estimate only; control_mcmc, if supplied, sets only the total number of predictive draws.

seed

Optional integer seed for random draws made during prediction, including a fresh conditional MCMC run. The caller's random-number state is restored on exit.

keep_samples

Logical. If TRUE, retain the minimal latent samples needed for custom post-processing. Predictive samples are generated to calculate summaries regardless of this setting, but are discarded by default to limit memory use.

messages

Logical. Display messages, and a progress bar while predicting at many locations, as described in riskmap_progress. Defaults to the option RiskMap.messages, or TRUE if it is not set.

...

Additional arguments reserved for future prediction methods.

Value

A RiskMap_prediction object containing:

predictions

The aligned prediction points or grid cells with their summaries.

boundaries

The supplied polygons, or NULL when no polygon aggregation was requested.

boundary_summary

For polygon prediction, a tidy table with one row per boundary, aggregation, component, summary and threshold. boundary_id is the row number of the corresponding polygon in boundaries.

samples

NULL when keep_samples = FALSE; otherwise a list containing spatial samples and any requested random-effect or nugget samples for location-level prediction, and, with parameter uncertainty, the fixed-effect contribution of each draw (fixed). For polygon aggregation it is nested first by aggregation and then by component, with one matrix row per polygon.

include

Optional components included in the link and response.

transform

Names of additional derived predictive targets.

standardized

Whether response predictions were averaged over a reference population supplied through standardize.

aggregate

Names of the within-polygon aggregations.

summaries

Names of the calculated summaries.

thresholds

Thresholds used for exceedance probabilities.

level

Probability covered by the interval limits.

weights

Name of the weights column used for the polygon summaries, or NULL.

type

Whether prediction was marginal or joint.

parameter_draws

The number of parameter draws when parameter uncertainty was propagated, otherwise NULL.

family

The fitted response family.

link

The link of the fit when it is not the canonical one, its name or "custom", and NULL for the canonical link.

response_name

Name of the response variable, used to label maps of Gaussian predictions.

observed_locations

Whether newdata was omitted.

coverage

NULL for location-only prediction. For polygon aggregation, "exact" when fractional grid-cell coverage was used and "point" for point-in-polygon assignment. This is output metadata, not a user-supplied argument.

Details

At new locations, the default prediction represents the underlying spatial surface, with linear predictor $$d(x)^T \hat\beta + S(x) + \mathrm{offset}(x).$$ The offset is included automatically when it was specified in the fitted model. Nugget and unstructured random effects are excluded unless requested explicitly because they generally represent observation-level or group-specific variation rather than the underlying spatial surface. The observed-location distinction for a fitted nugget is described below.

For non-Gaussian fits, stored final-parameter conditional samples are reused when control_mcmc = NULL. If the model was fitted with return_samples = FALSE, the function draws a new conditional sample using set_control_mcmc() defaults. Supplying control_mcmc always requests a fresh conditional run. For Gaussian models, prediction is based on their exact conditional Gaussian distribution.

Plug-in prediction treats the estimated parameters as known, so its intervals can be too narrow when the parameters, in particular the spatial variance and scale, are poorly estimated, as in small or low-prevalence surveys. With parameter_uncertainty = TRUE, parameter_draws parameter values are drawn from the approximate sampling distribution of the estimate: a multivariate normal distribution with the estimated covariance matrix, on the scale on which the model is estimated (log variances and log scale). For each value, conditional samples of the latent effects are generated at that value and the prediction is repeated; the draws are then pooled, so every summary, aggregation and derived target reflects both the latent and the parameter uncertainty. For binomial, Poisson and negative binomial models the conditional samples at each parameter value come from a short run of the same Langevin (MALA) sampler used for plug-in prediction, in coordinates whitened by the Laplace approximation at that value, started from a draw of that approximation and using the step size tuned at the estimate (100 burn-in iterations, then thinning by 10). The total number of predictive draws equals that of plug-in prediction, 2,000 by default. Parameters without a finite positive variance, such as those held at a boundary, keep their estimated value. When the covariance matrix of the estimates is not available, an error is returned; refitting with set_control_mcml(pc_prior = TRUE) usually resolves this. The location column fixed then reports the average fixed-effect contribution.

At the observed locations, the conditioned location-level Gaussian effect already includes the fitted nugget when the model has one. Consequently, include = "nugget" is available only for predictions supplied through newdata, where it represents a new independent nugget realization.

newdata and boundaries are transformed internally to the fitted model CRS without changing row order; returned geometries remain in their input CRS. Rows with missing required predictors are retained with NA predictions and an informative warning.

When boundaries are supplied, one prediction run produces both the location-level output in predictions and the areal output in boundary_summary. Joint samples are generated in the smallest independent blocks that preserve dependence within every polygon. Polygons sharing a fractionally covered grid cell are placed in the same block so that the cell's draw is reused rather than simulated twice. This avoids constructing a full joint covariance over unrelated prediction locations. Locations outside all polygons remain in predictions but do not contribute to areal aggregation; polygons with no usable locations remain in boundaries with NA summaries.

With location weights \(w_i\), "mean" computes $$\sum_i w_i T_i / \sum_i w_i,$$ so population values are converted internally to within-polygon fractions. "sum" instead computes \(\sum_i w_i T_i\) and never normalizes the weights. Thus, a prevalence prediction weighted by population counts gives population-weighted prevalence under "mean" and expected cases under "sum". Population densities must first be multiplied by the represented cell areas. When newdata was created by create_grid(), each supplied weight is multiplied by the exact fraction of its square cell covered by each polygon. Cells crossing a boundary can therefore contribute to more than one polygon. For an arbitrary sf point object, cell footprints cannot be inferred safely and each point is assigned to the polygon containing it.

For location-level prediction, output columns use <quantity>_<summary> names. For example, response_mean, response_lower, and response_upper describe the response-scale prediction, while the corresponding spatial_* and link_* columns describe the spatial process and complete linear predictor. fixed is the estimated fixed-effects contribution and offset is reported separately. When requested through include, random_effects_* and nugget_* report those contributions separately as well as incorporating them into link_* and response_*. Binomial response predictions are probabilities and Poisson response predictions are rates per unit exposure.

Derived targets supplied through transform are evaluated draw by draw before any location-level summary or polygon aggregation. Their output uses the target name as the quantity prefix. With multiple thresholds, location-level exceedance columns are named, for example, response_exceedance_0.2 and response_exceedance_0.5; polygon output stores thresholds in the tidy threshold column.

When standardize is supplied, every conditional spatial draw is reused across all rows of the reference population. The response and any derived targets are evaluated for each reference profile and then averaged using .weight. This is direct standardization (empirical or counterfactual averaging), not simulation of uncertain predictors. The reported fixed and link_* quantities use the weighted mean fixed-effect contribution; with a nonlinear link, transforming that mean is not the same as the standardized response_* quantity.

See also

glgpm(), fitted(), set_control_mcmc()

Examples

data(italy_sim)
example_data <- italy_sim[1:50, ]
fit <- glgpm(y ~ pop_dens + gp(), data = example_data, family = "gaussian",
             messages = FALSE)

# Calculate an additional predictive target from every linear-predictor draw
prediction <- predict(
  fit,
  newdata = example_data[1:5, ],
  transform = list(squared_link = function(link) link^2),
  messages = FALSE
)
prediction$predictions
#> Simple feature collection with 5 features and 19 fields

#> * <dbl> <fct>   <fct>       <dbl>  <int>        <POINT [m]> <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1  6.74 Toscana Pisa         536.      1 (165557.8 4845668)  8.63      0
#> 2  8.56 Toscana Pisa         536.      1 (165557.8 4845668)  8.63      0
#> 3  8.05 Toscana Pisa         536.      1 (165557.8 4845668)  8.63      0
#> 4  7.53 Toscana Pisa         536.      1 (165557.8 4845668)  8.63      0
#> 5  7.16 Toscana Pisa         536.      1 (165557.8 4845668)  8.63      0
#> # ℹ 12 more variables: spatial_mean <dbl>, spatial_lower <dbl>,
#> #   spatial_upper <dbl>, link_mean <dbl>, link_lower <dbl>, link_upper <dbl>,
#> #   response_mean <dbl>, response_lower <dbl>, response_upper <dbl>,
#> #   squared_link_mean <dbl>, squared_link_lower <dbl>, squared_link_upper <dbl>

# Also reflect the uncertainty in the estimated parameters
uncertain_prediction <- predict(
  fit,
  newdata = example_data[1:5, ],
  parameter_uncertainty = TRUE,
  parameter_draws = 20,
  messages = FALSE
)
uncertain_prediction$predictions

# Use the same reference distribution of population density at each location
reference_population <- data.frame(pop_dens = example_data$pop_dens)
standardized_prediction <- predict(
  fit,
  newdata = example_data[1:5, ],
  standardize = reference_population,
  messages = FALSE
)
standardized_prediction$predictions

# Aggregate joint predictions within two example areas
areas <- sf::st_sf(
  area = 1:2,
  geometry = sf::st_make_grid(example_data, n = c(2, 1))
)
areal_prediction <- predict(
  fit,
  newdata = example_data,
  boundaries = areas,
  aggregate = "mean",
  messages = FALSE
)
